articles.title: National Mammography Day: Four Screening Myths That Keep Women From Getting Checked
articles.excerpt: Most breast cancers are found in women with no family history, mammograms miss about one in five cancers, and implants are no barrier — what clinicians want women to know on October 16.
articles.image_caption: A mammogram screening in progress. National Mammography Day, on October 16 this year, is a prompt to book screening rather than wait for symptoms.
articles.nri_angle: Breast cancer strikes Indian women about a decade earlier than Western averages, making family-history-based complacency especially risky for diaspora readers.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

items: Myth 1: No family history, no risk.
Myth 4: I can stop at my age.

articles.title: Yuzvendra Chahal Says Rehab Followed Drinking That Crossed All Limits
articles.excerpt: The India leg-spinner told Aakash Chopra's podcast that he spent 26 days in a rehabilitation centre after his divorce, and described the anxiety attacks that came with that period.
articles.nri_angle: A senior India cricketer describing rehab and anxiety in detail gives diaspora readers a factual, stigma-free account of seeking professional help after a personal crisis.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Fibremaxing With Indian Food: Dal and Millets Beat Imported Powders
articles.excerpt: The viral trend urges maximising fibre toward the 25-38 gram daily target most adults miss. Traditional Indian staples — dals, millets, vegetables and guava — already do the job, if intake rises gradually.
articles.image_caption: Dal makhani (file photo). Traditional dals and millets are central to the fibremaxing trend.
articles.nri_angle: Diaspora readers can follow the fibre trend with familiar Indian staples — dal, millets and guava — instead of imported supplements, closing a typical 10-23 gram daily shortfall.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Breast Cancer Hits Indian Women a Decade Earlier: When to Screen
articles.excerpt: Average diagnosis in India is around 47, versus about 60 in the West. Oncologists lay out a screening ladder — self-exams from 21, clinical exams, and mammograms from the 40s — and why family history moves the timetable up.
articles.nri_angle: Indian-American women should follow the US mammogram schedule from age 40 while flagging early diagnoses among relatives in India, which can move their personal screening timetable earlier.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: WHO Says Childhood Obesity Needs More Than Medicine: A Family-First Plan
articles.excerpt: WHO's first global childhood obesity guidelines bar drugs and surgery for under-10s and put diet, activity, sleep and caregiver support first for all ages.
articles.image_caption: Childhood obesity is rising worldwide. The WHO says tackling it needs a family-first plan that goes beyond medicine alone.
articles.nri_angle: Indian diaspora families facing the same school, screen and snack pressures can apply WHO's sequence at home: shared meals and daily activity first, medicines only on specialist advice for older adolescents.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A 'Pinch Me Moment': Kyle Clark Lands His Dream Netflix Lead in 'How to Ruin Diwali'
articles.excerpt: The South African presenter-turned-actor stars opposite Rosemary Zimu-Mnguni in Netflix's three-episode Diwali comedy, premiering October 30 — a meet-the-parents clash of African and Indian families from the makers of the Kandasamys films.
articles.image_caption: Diwali diyas. Kyle Clark stars in the Netflix film 'How to Ruin Diwali' in his first lead role.
articles.nri_angle: For Indian families in South Africa and the wider diaspora, the series puts a Diwali household — complete with a traditional Indian family at its centre — at the heart of a mainstream Netflix comedy, streaming globally from October 30.

articles.title: Bommai Kolu: A Diaspora Guide to South India's Navratri Doll Display
articles.excerpt: From the kalasam on the top step to the marapachi couple, how Tamil, Telugu and Kannada families build the tiered doll court that anchors Navratri — and how to start one in a US or UK home.
articles.nri_angle: Kolu is one of the most portable Navratri traditions: a three-step starter display, a pair of marapachi dolls and nightly sundal will recreate it in any diaspora apartment.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

steps.detail: Kolu is arranged on an odd number of tiers — 3, 5, 7, 9 or 11. First-timers can start with 3 or 5 using a stand, stacked boxes or a bookshelf covered with cloth.
Fill a pot with water and rice, add betel leaves, a coin and turmeric, ring the mouth with mango leaves and top with a turmeric-smeared coconut. Light a lamp before placing any dolls.
The wooden bride-and-groom pair, often passed down through generations, goes on the top steps first.
Deities and sacred figures take the upper tiers; saints, wedding scenes, animals and everyday life fill the steps below.

steps.step: Add one new doll each year
steps.detail: The annual addition marks abundance and keeps the display growing with the family.

steps.step: Host and visit through the nine nights
steps.detail: Invite friends and neighbours to view the display, sing devotional songs and share prasadam such as sundal.

articles.title: Normal Cholesterol, Hidden Heart Risk: The Tests Your Lipid Panel Misses
articles.excerpt: More than 5,000 Indian first-heart-attack patients were never flagged as high-risk by standard calculators — about 8 in 10 were classified low or moderate. Three tests beyond the lipid panel — ApoB, Lp(a), and a coronary calcium scan — reveal the risk a "normal" cholesterol report hides.
articles.image_caption: A home blood-pressure monitor displays an elevated reading. Cardiologists say a single "normal" result — whether blood pressure or a standard lipid panel — does not guarantee the heart is safe.
articles.nri_angle: South Asians in the US/UK develop heart disease 5-10 years earlier and are underestimated by Western calculators; the article tells diaspora readers exactly which tests to ask their doctor for.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Normal BMI, Hidden Diabetes: Why Young Indians Need Metabolic Screening
articles.excerpt: New Indian data shows diabetes is striking people in their 20s and 30s — often slim ones. The ICMR-INDIAB study found 43.3% of adults were metabolically obese despite a normal BMI, and one in five under-30s in a 3-million-person Apollo dataset was prediabetic.
articles.image_caption: A person holds a takeaway salad bowl with chicken and vegetables. Experts say diet quality, adequate protein, and muscle-building exercise matter more for metabolic health than the number on the scale.
articles.nri_angle: South Asians abroad develop diabetes nearly a decade earlier than Europeans, yet Western BMI cutoffs give diaspora patients false reassurance; the article tells them to ask their doctor for South Asian thresholds plus a metabolic panel.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: UP Cities Get Cleanliness and Lighting Makeover Ahead of Diwali and Chhath

articles.title: Navratri 2026: Devotional Bhajans for Nine Mornings of Maa Durga Worship

articles.title: HPV Vaccine Before Pregnancy Linked to Lower Preterm Birth Risk
articles.excerpt: A Swedish study of 624,713 births, published in The BMJ, found mothers vaccinated against HPV before pregnancy had lower odds of preterm birth and other complications — an observational finding that stops short of proof.
articles.image_caption: Gardasil, the HPV vaccine
articles.nri_angle: Cervical cancer is a leading cause of cancer death among women in India, and this study gives Indian families one more evidence-backed reason to vaccinate adolescents early — adding potential pregnancy-health benefits to the established cancer protection.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Mediterranean and MIND Diets Linked to Better Cognitive Performance
articles.excerpt: A pooled analysis of 17,368 participants across Europe and the US found continuous Mediterranean, DASH and MIND diets tied to sharper thinking — but only MIND held up over time.
articles.image_caption: A bowl of green grapes sits alongside milk, bananas, and apples on an outdoor table. A 2026 meta-analysis of 17,368 people linked Mediterranean and MIND diet patterns to better cognitive performance.
articles.nri_angle: Everyday Indian cooking — lentils, leafy greens like palak and methi, vegetables, modest meat — already mirrors the MIND diet pattern, giving diaspora readers a familiar, practical frame for the study's findings rather than an imported Mediterranean shopping list.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Dating Apps Go Offline in India as Singles Tire of the Swipe
articles.excerpt: Match Group's The League, Bumble and Tinder are betting on real-world mixers — singles runs, pickleball, curated dinners — after surveys show Indian users want conversations that outlast small talk. But veterans of the mixer circuit say the offline economy has problems of its own.
articles.image_caption: Singles at a speed-dating event at a Nairobi hotel. Dating apps including Bumble and Tinder are expanding into real-world singles events in India as users report fatigue with app-based matchmaking. (Representative photo, Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian diaspora singles in cities like New York, San Francisco and Toronto report the same swipe fatigue layered over community marriage expectations, and the hybrid offline-event model emerging in India may prove directly exportable to diaspora meetup culture.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: PCOS Is Now PMOS: What the New Name Means for Women's Diagnosis
articles.excerpt: A global medical consensus published in The Lancet in May 2026 has renamed polycystic ovary syndrome as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome — a shift experts say could speed up diagnosis and ease stigma for the 170 million women affected.
articles.image_caption: An editorial illustration about women's reproductive health. Polycystic ovary syndrome has been renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), a change experts say could speed up diagnosis for the roughly 170 million women affected worldwide.
articles.nri_angle: South Asian women face higher metabolic complications at lower BMIs, so diaspora women should ensure insulin-resistance screening is part of their care; the rename also eases the marriageability-and-fertility stigma many Indian families attach to the condition.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Well-Prepared for Plague, but Early Diagnosis Is Key, Expert Says
articles.excerpt: After a suspected pneumonic plague death in Siberia rattled global headlines, IMA Research Cell convenor Dr Rajeev Jayadevan told ANI there is no immediate threat to India — and urged vigilance over alarm.
articles.image_caption: A fluorescent micrograph of Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague. A suspected pneumonic plague death in Russia's Irkutsk region has put global health watchers on alert.
articles.nri_angle: Indian travellers and the diaspora in Russia need not panic over the Siberian case — experts say severe pneumonic plague patients are rarely well enough to travel far, and India runs dedicated plague surveillance at home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Pomegranate Compound May Improve Stiff-Heart Failure, Study Finds
articles.excerpt: King's College London researchers found that urolithin A, made by gut bacteria after eating pomegranates, improved heart function up to 80% in animal models of stiff-heart failure by activating a key relaxation protein.
articles.image_caption: A close-up of pomegranate seeds. Researchers at Kings College London found that urolithin A, produced by gut bacteria after eating pomegranates, improved heart function in animal models of stiff-heart failure.
articles.nri_angle: Pomegranate is a familiar staple in Indian kitchens and Ayurvedic tradition, making this study culturally resonant — though the honest read is that it validates a biochemical pathway, not a traditional remedy.

articles.title: Indian Mom Harshana Loses 32 Kg in 11 Months, Quits Five Everyday Foods
articles.excerpt: Gurugram-based work-from-home mother Deepti Harshana shared the everyday foods she quit — sugary drinks, white bread, packaged snacks, fried food and late-night snacking — alongside hydration, sleep and daily walking.

articles.title: Delhi Terrace With 500 Native Plants Now Draws 100 Bird Species
articles.excerpt: Conservationist Aman Sharma turned a bare rooftop into an urban ecosystem during the 2020 lockdown — and shared a three-plant formula anyone can copy, starting with a single host plant.
articles.image_caption: Aman Sharma holds a potted plant on his rooftop terrace in Delhi, surrounded by the dense planting he built up since 2020. The terrace now holds more than 500 native plants and has documented over 100 bird species.

articles.title: Delhi Dementia Conclave Urges Prevention, Caregiver Support as Cases Head Toward 17 Million
articles.excerpt: Experts at the Hope for Dementia Conclave 2026 warned that dementia cases in India could nearly double to 16.9 million by 2036, calling for prevention, early diagnosis and caregiver support to become public health priorities.
articles.image_caption: The Hope for Dementia Conclave 2026 in New Delhi urged prevention, early identification and caregiver support as India's dementia cases head toward 17 million by 2036
articles.nri_angle: Millions of NRIs coordinate care for ageing parents in India from abroad; the conclave's push for early diagnosis, caregiver training and community-level support speaks directly to the logistics and costs of long-distance caregiving.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Trehan to Young Indians: Get a Heart Check-Up Before 25
articles.excerpt: On World Heart Day, leading cardiologists told PTI that heart disease is striking Indians younger — and that screening should start at 25 or 30, not in middle age.
articles.image_caption: Naresh Trehan, chairman and managing director of Medanta, who urged young Indians to get a heart check-up before 25
articles.nri_angle: The heart-disease risk profile doesn't change at the airport: diaspora families eating Western diets face compounded risk, making Trehan's 'check-up before 25/30' rule as relevant in Surrey or Edison as in Surat.
